scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): concedes the appeal of rewarding good teaching, then shows why pay tied mainly to student scores is unfair; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: It seems only fair to reward teachers whose students do well.
Some people claim that teachers' salaries should be based on how their students perform academically.
I agree that good teaching should be rewarded, but I believe basing salaries mainly on student results would be unfair and harmful.

sections.role: Body 1 — The appeal of the idea

sentences.text: First, the idea does contain a reasonable goal, which is to encourage good teaching.
Linking some reward to performance might push teachers to prepare more carefully and support struggling students.
For example, a school that recognises its excellent teachers can motivate others to improve.
This shows that rewarding effort and skill is not wrong in itself.
Students clearly deserve teachers who are encouraged to do their very best.
Modest bonuses for outstanding work could be one fair way to value the profession.
To this extent, the claim rests on a sensible instinct.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why it would be unfair

sentences.text: Second, however, student results depend on far more than the teacher alone.
A child's home life, health, and background all strongly affect how well she learns.
Consider two teachers of equal skill, one in a wealthy school and one in a poor neighbourhood with few resources.
Judging them by results alone would punish the second teacher for problems beyond her control.
Such a system could also push teachers to focus only on tests, by contrast neglecting creativity and slower learners.
Some might even avoid the struggling students who need them most.
Pay tied mainly to scores would therefore harm fairness and learning at once.
In conclusion, rewarding good teaching is a fair aim, and modest bonuses may help.
But basing salaries mainly on student performance would ignore everything else that shapes results.
A wiser system judges teachers by the quality of their work, not only by the scores of their students.
